description: Self-hosted rebuild of Grafana Cloud's Temporal overview. Cloud-only rows (billable actions, TRU capacity, action limits, replication lag, schedules) removed; see docs/CLOUD-TO-SELFHOSTED.md for the full mapping.

panels.title: Running executions
panels.description:
Open Workflow Executions, from the Visibility monitor in monitor/.

Cloud reads temporal_cloud_v1_namespace_open_workflows. Self-hosted has no such gauge — nothing in Prometheus counts executions that have not ended, which is the entire reason monitor/ exists.

'monitor down?' means the monitor is not running, NOT that there is no work.

panels.title: Completions / sec
panels.description: Successful Workflow completions per second. Server counter + rate(), NOT a Cloud gauge.

panels.title: Frontend req / sec
panels.description:
All Frontend RPCs per second, long-polls included.

Closest analogue to the Cloud board's Actions/sec — but NOT the same thing. Actions are a billing unit; this is request volume.

panels.title: Tasks with no poller
panels.description:
Tasks queued to a Task Queue NOBODY is polling.

The self-hosted stand-in for the Cloud backlog gauge. Anything above zero is work that waits until a Worker appears — and every other panel stays green while it does.

panels.title: Sync match rate
panels.description:
Tasks handed straight to a waiting Worker vs persisted first. High is good.

Replaces the Cloud board's backlog stat: a falling sync match rate is the earliest sign the fleet is behind, and it LEADS schedule-to-start latency.

panels.title: Pending requests
panels.description:
Frontend requests in flight. A GAUGE, so no rate().

The one Cloud stat that ports almost unchanged — service_pending_requests exists on both.

panels.title: Completions by outcome
panels.description:
The Cloud board splits these across five panels (success/failed/timeout/cancel/continued-as-new). One panel, because the comparison IS the signal.

WATCH TIMEOUT. Saturation on Temporal produces TIMEOUTS, not failures: under a backlog storm workflow_failed sat at 0.02/s while workflow_timeout hit 24.6/s. An SLI watching only failures reported ~100% healthy while three quarters of all work expired.

EXPECT ONLY 'success' ON A HEALTHY STACK — these counters do not exist in Prometheus until they first increment. `make chaos-failures` and `make chaos-backlog` create them.

NOT INCLUDED: workflow_cancel and workflow_continued_as_new, which the Cloud board plots. Neither was observable on this 1.27.4 deployment, and a panel querying a metric that may never exist is worse than an honest omission.

panels.title: Completions by Task Queue
panels.description:
Cloud groups this by temporal_task_queue. The self-hosted server label is `taskqueue` — ONE WORD, NO UNDERSCORE — while the Go/Java SDK uses `task_queue`. Mixing them gives an empty panel with no error.

The Cloud original also offers by-workflow-type. Self-hosted server completion counters carry no workflow-type label, so that breakdown lives in the SDK metrics below.

panels.title: Workflow end-to-end latency
panels.description:
Workflow latency percentiles, inclusive of retries and backoff — the Cloud board's three separate p50/p95/p99 panels collapsed into one.

SDK metric, so this is what YOUR WORKERS observed. Seconds on Go and Java; TypeScript, Python and .NET emit milliseconds and this panel is then wrong by 1000x. Run `make verify-sdk-labels`.

panels.title: Workflow task execution latency
panels.description:
How long a single Workflow Task took to execute.

Not on the Cloud board, and it belongs here: this is where sticky-cache evictions surface. A forced eviction means the next Workflow Task REPLAYS the whole history instead of resuming, which shows up as latency here and as nothing at all in the completion counters.

panels.title: Activity execution latency (SDK)
panels.description:
Time spent RUNNING an Activity, excluding queue wait. SDK-side.

This is the panel people expect to move during a backlog and it does not — queue wait is schedule-to-start, in the Pollers row. An Activity can execute in 3ms while the fleet is minutes behind.

panels.title: Activity end-to-end latency (server)
panels.description:
Schedule-to-close as the SERVER sees it: queue wait plus execution plus retries and backoff. The Cloud board's activity_schedule_to_close_latency.

The gap between this and the SDK panel to the left IS the queue wait. When they diverge, add Workers.

LABEL TRAP: this server metric carries camelCase `activityType`/`workflowType`, while the SDK metric beside it uses snake_case `activity_type`/`workflow_type`. Same concept, different spelling, silently empty if you mix them.

panels.title: Activity failures and retries
panels.description:
Activity executions that failed, per second, by type.

The Cloud board separates 'Failures' from 'Failures including retries' using two distinct metrics. The Go SDK exposes only temporal_activity_execution_failed_total, which counts EVERY failed attempt — so this is the 'including retries' number. There is no self-hosted equivalent of the retries-excluded panel.

A retry storm looks like this metric rising while workflow completions stay flat.

panels.title: Activity poll efficiency
panels.description:
Polls that timed out with no Activity Task, and the number of pollers running.

High no-task rate with steady pollers is a fleet that is OVER-provisioned for current load — the opposite problem to a backlog, and the one nobody looks for. Near-zero no-task rate means pollers never idle, which means work is queuing.

panels.title: Poll outcomes
panels.description:
The Cloud board's four poller stat tiles as one comparison.

METRIC NAME TRAP: the self-hosted counter is `poll_timeouts` — PLURAL. `poll_timeout` does not exist and returns nothing.

A poll timeout is NORMAL: a poller waited its full long-poll window and no work arrived. Timeouts dominating means an idle cluster, not a broken one.

panels.title: Sync match rate by Task Queue
panels.description: Per-queue sync match. This is where a single starved Task Queue shows up while the cluster-wide number still looks fine.

panels.title: Schedule-to-start p99
panels.description:
How long a Task waits before a Worker picks it up. THE fleet-capacity signal, and the one to autoscale on.

NEVER AUTOSCALE A WORKER ON CPU. A Worker blocked in a long poll uses almost no CPU, so when the queue backs up CPU stays flat or FALLS — a CPU-based autoscaler then scales down the fleet that is already behind. It is not a weak signal, it is an inverted one.

panels.title: Worker slots and sticky cache

targets.expr:
sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_used{namespace=~"$namespace"})
/ clamp_min(
    sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_used{namespace=~"$namespace"})
  + sum by (task_queue) (temporal_worker_task_slots_available{namespace=~"$namespace"}), 1)

panels.description:
Worker slot utilisation per Task Queue (SDK label `task_queue`, underscore — unlike the server's `taskqueue`), plus forced sticky-cache evictions.

At 100% slots with LOW host CPU: raise MaxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize, do not add Workers. At 100% with HIGH host CPU: add Workers. The discriminator is host CPU, which is NOT a Temporal metric — you need node_exporter or cAdvisor or the two cases are indistinguishable.

Evictions are plotted here because they are the hidden cost of a cache that is too small: every eviction forces a full history replay on the next Workflow Task.

panels.title: Requests by operation
panels.description:
Top 8 Frontend operations.

The Cloud board pairs this with a request LIMIT line (temporal_cloud_v1_service_request_limit). Self-hosted has no per-namespace rate limit to plot — you are the capacity. The equivalent question is answered by the Persistence row below.

Poll* dominating is correct. Its ABSENCE is the alarm.

panels.title: Errors by type — server fault only
panels.description:
Frontend errors by type, CLIENT faults filtered out.

The filter is measured, not stylistic: Matching emits a steady ~0.39/s of serviceerror_Canceled at idle. Counting it took availability to 98.77% and blew a 99.9% budget many times over while nothing was wrong.

Empty is the healthy state.

panels.title: Frontend latency (long-polls excluded)
panels.description:
Frontend latency percentiles with long-polls excluded.

PollWorkflowTaskQueue and PollActivityTaskQueue block up to 60s by design and are the highest-volume operations. Included: 95.9% of requests 'under 500ms'. Excluded: 100%. The unfiltered version fires a latency alert forever on a healthy idle cluster.

panels.title: Resource exhausted
panels.description:
Requests rejected because a limit was hit, broken down by CAUSE.

The Cloud board plots this too, and it is the one 'quota' panel that survives translation — self-hosted has no per-namespace billing quota, but it does have rate limiters, and resource_exhausted_cause tells you which one fired (RpsLimit, ConcurrentLimit, SystemOverloaded, PersistenceLimit).

This is the panel to check before concluding the datastore is slow.

panels.title: StartWorkflowExecution latency
panels.description:
The Cloud board's Service Operations row, kept in full — these three operations are the ones a caller actually feels.

StartWorkflowExecution latency is what your API sees when it kicks off work.

panels.title: SignalWorkflowExecution latency
panels.description: Signal delivery latency. Empty until something signals — this stack's demo app does not, so an empty panel here is correct rather than broken.

panels.title: SignalWithStartWorkflowExecution latency
panels.description: Signal-with-start latency. Also empty unless your application uses the pattern.

panels.title: Persistence and shards  ·  replaces the Cloud usage, billing and TRU rows
Persistence latency
panels.description:
Datastore latency percentiles.

CHECK THIS BEFORE SCALING ANY TEMPORAL SERVICE. Persistence is upstream of nearly every Temporal latency symptom, and adding Frontend or History replicas against a saturated datastore makes it worse.

panels.title: Persistence latency p95 by operation
panels.description: Which datastore operation is slow. CreateWorkflowExecution and UpdateWorkflowExecution dominating is normal; GetTasks or RangeCompleteHistoryTasks climbing usually means queue processing is falling behind.

panels.title: Persistence errors and request rate
panels.description:
Datastore throughput against datastore failures.

Any sustained error rate here is the root cause of whatever else you are looking at. Errors with a flat request rate points at the datastore; errors that track request rate points at capacity.

panels.title: Shard queue lag p95
panels.description:
How far behind the History service's internal task queues are.

No Cloud equivalent — Temporal operates the shards for you there. Self-hosted, this is the earliest warning that the History service cannot keep up, and it moves well before user-visible latency does.

Sustained growth means timers and transfer tasks are being processed late, which surfaces to users as Workflows that start late for no visible reason.
